primary_claim: Top-down activation steering (contrastive refusal-direction) outperforms bottom-up SAE-based steering at bypassing refusal on harmful prompts in Qwen 1.5 0.5B, but a hybrid method combining both further outperforms top-down alone, at some cost to benign capabilities.

effect.metric: relative improvement in bypassing refusal on HarmBench
effect.value: top-down ~93% relative improvement over bottom-up (~1.93x more effective); hybrid ~35% relative improvement over top-down (~1.85x), 85% for harmful instructions only

contradicts_or_qualifies: In line with prior work (Brumley et al. 2024; Kissane et al. 2024; O'Brien et al. 2024), confirms that top-down steering outperforms bottom-up SAE-based steering
stated_future_work: Try other harm-related SAE features and investigate combining them (multi-feature steering) to reduce the performance penalty
Systematically evaluate which layers' directions matter most for refusal and behaviour steering (layer-by-layer analysis)
Extend experiments to significantly larger LLMs (scaling studies)
Use more benchmarks (e.g. Llama Guard) and adversarial prompts to measure robustness of each steering method
limitations_stated: Tested on a relatively small model (Qwen1.5 500M); results may differ for larger systems, though related research on a bigger model (Phi3 3.8B) shows analogous trends
Did not optimize layer choice or steering coefficients (minimal hyperparameter tuning)
Evaluation scope limited; more robust evaluation across datasets and models needed to clarify generalization
quote: experiments show that top-down methods outperform bottom-up ones in behaviour steering (93% relative improvement), but a hybrid approach is even more effective (~35% relative improvement compared to top-down).
